title: Rival Sisters and a Shepherd's Deal
overview: Rachel and Leah compete for Jacob through having children, and then Jacob strikes a wage deal with Laban that leaves him wealthy.

parts.label: Rachel's desperate plan (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: In that culture, being unable to have children brought deep shame, so Rachel gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob and counts the children as her own, a custom also seen with Sarah and Hagar. She names the boys Dan, meaning 'vindicated,' and Naphtali, meaning 'my wrestling,' names that keep score against her sister.

parts.label: Leah answers in kind (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: When Leah stops having children, she does the same with her servant Zilpah and names the sons Gad, 'good fortune,' and Asher, 'happy.' The text never records what Bilhah or Zilpah thought of being used this way.

parts.label: The mandrake bargain (vv. 14-21)
parts.note: Mandrakes were plants widely believed to help women conceive, and Rachel trades a night with Jacob to get some, which may suggest Jacob had been spending more of his nights with her. The irony is that Leah, who gave the plants up, is the one who conceives, naming her sons Issachar, which sounds like 'reward,' and Zebulun, which plays on 'honor.'

parts.label: Rachel finally has a son (vv. 22-24)
parts.note: The story credits God, not the mandrakes, when Rachel at last gives birth. She names him Joseph, which sounds like 'may he add,' as she hopes for another son.

parts.label: Jacob's deal with Laban (vv. 25-36)
parts.note: Jacob wants to go home, but Laban admits he has prospered because of Jacob and asks him to stay. Sheep there were usually white and goats dark, so Jacob asks only for the rare spotted or dark animals, and that same day all such animals already in the flock are removed and handed to Laban's sons, three days' journey away.

parts.label: Striped branches, growing flocks (vv. 37-43)
parts.note: Jacob sets peeled, striped branches before the stronger animals as they mate, reflecting an old folk belief that what a mother sees shapes her young, so the strong offspring become his and the weak ones Laban's. Peeled branches do not actually change offspring, and in the next chapter Jacob credits God for the outcome, so readers debate how much was skill, trickery, or blessing.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jacob's breeding scheme should be read as quiet trickery that the story does not approve, or as God's fair provision for a worker whom Laban had treated unfairly.
think: When two people compete for the same love or recognition, what tends to happen to the people caught in between?
